title: Pseudocereals: Quinoa, Amaranth, and Buckwheat

seo.title: Pseudocereals: Quinoa, Amaranth, and Buckwheat
seo.meta_description: Quinoa, amaranth, and buckwheat are non-grass seeds used like grains. All are naturally gluten-free and provide different mixes of protein, fiber, and minerals.
seo.search_intent: Understand what pseudocereals are and compare quinoa, amaranth, and buckwheat.

excerpt: Quinoa, amaranth, and buckwheat are not botanical cereal grains. They are seeds from non-grass plants that are cooked and milled in grain-like ways. All three are naturally gluten-free, with distinct textures and nutrient profiles.
content_html:
Pseudocereal is a practical botanical term, not a health-marketing category. These foods are seeds from non-grass plants that are used like cereal grains.

Quinoa

Cooked quinoa is about 120 calories, 4.4 g protein, and 2.8 g fiber per 100 g. It has a balanced essential-amino-acid profile and a relatively neutral texture.

Amaranth

Cooked amaranth is about 100 calories and 3.8 g protein per 100 g. It tends to cook into a creamier texture and contributes calcium, iron, and magnesium.

Buckwheat

Cooked buckwheat groats are roughly 90–95 calories, 3–4 g protein, and close to 3 g fiber per 100 g. The flavor is nuttier and more toasted.

All three are naturally gluten-free

The Celiac Disease Foundation lists quinoa, amaranth, and buckwheat among naturally gluten-free foods, though cross-contact still matters for celiac disease.

Pseudocereal means used like a grain, not nutritionally identical to every other pseudocereal.

faq.question: Are pseudocereals gluten-free?
faq.answer: Quinoa, amaranth, and buckwheat are naturally gluten-free, although cross-contact can occur.

faq.question: Are they seeds?
faq.answer: Yes. Botanically they are seeds from plants outside the grass family.

faq.question: Which has the most protein?
faq.answer: By cooked weight the differences are modest; quinoa is around 4.4 g/100 g, amaranth about 3.8 g, and buckwheat about 3–4 g.
